tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, table, diagram, collage, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final text reply; call it before writing that reply. The reader already sees the page, so the reply should not announce it, say where it is, or restate it: add only what the page doesn't say. Preview with html_preview first. T3 fits the frame to the page's height at each reader's width. A height below the page's contentHeight caps the frame there, and the rest scrolls inside it. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The frame is borderless on the thread's background, as wide as the reply column (728px on desktop by default, wider if the reader widens chat, about 360px on phones), and its left edge lines up with your reply text. The page sits on the thread's own background, so by default leave html, body, and the outermost element with no background color. This overrides general style preferences such as a fixed black page background. Use a fluid width with no horizontal padding on the outermost element, and no outer card, border, or banner title: the page is part of your reply. If a box needs its own background (a mock of a specific screen, a panel that must stand apart), give it at least 16px of padding on every side and var(--radius) corners, so content never touches its edge. Give charts fixed pixel heights rather than heights that scale with width. Let content set the page's height. Avoid viewport-based heights such as 100vh or height:100% on html or body; the frame grows to fit the page, so they can make it grow again and again. T3 injects its active theme as CSS custom properties on :root, and they follow the user's theme and light/dark mode live: --background (page background, identical to the thread around the frame), --foreground, --muted, --muted-foreground, --card, --card-foreground, --popover, --popover-foreground, --secondary, --secondary-foreground, --border, --input, --ring, --primary, --primary-foreground (solid buttons), --accent, --accent-foreground (brand accent), --accent-surface, --accent-surface-foreground, --destructive, --destructive-foreground, --destructive-surface, --warning, --warning-foreground, --warning-surface, --success, --success-foreground, --info, --info-foreground, --code-background, --code-foreground, --chart-1 ... --chart-6 (categorical series for charts), --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base stylesheet sets html background/color/font from these, body margin to 0, and hides the page's scrollbar; your own CSS overrides it.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__schedule_task
tools.description: Create persistent work in the app scheduler that runs even when no turn is active. Pass schedule as a STRUCTURED OBJECT, never JSON text. Timers: {type:'interval', everyMs:3600000} is hourly; {type:'fixed_time', timeOfDay:'09:00', weekdays:[1,2,3,4,5]} is weekday mornings; report the returned nextRunAt. Webhooks: {type:'webhook'} runs once per request to a generated URL. The run sees the request ONLY through prompt placeholders: {{body.path}} (e.g. {{body.action}}, {{body.release.tag_name}}), {{headers.name}}, {{query.name}}, {{body}}, or {{request}} (method, headers with credentials redacted, and body). For a sender that signs requests, first call request_secret so the user enters the secret privately (never ask for it in chat or invent one), then set signature with the returned secretRef, e.g. GitHub: {type:'webhook', signature:{header:'x-hub-signature-256', encoding:'hex', prefix:'sha256=', secretRef}}. The result's webhookUrl is the public URL to give the user; if it is absent, this environment has no T3 Connect managed tunnel, so tell the user to enable T3 Connect remote access rather than sharing a path. Omit projectId for this thread's project. In this thread's project, runs post into THIS thread by default (bindToCurrentThread=true), which suits an orchestrator that sees every trigger, delegates work, and can dedupe against what is in flight; use false only when the user wants a fresh top-level thread per run. Elsewhere each run launches a fresh thread. Provider, model, and runtime settings inherit from this thread, or from the project default when there is no calling thread.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_launch
tools.description: Create an ordinary TOP-LEVEL thread with an explicit workspace binding before its agent starts. Use this when the user requests independent work, a new thread, or a PR stack in its own worktree; use delegate_task for child subagents. Set workspaceStrategy to {type:"worktree",baseRef:"parent-branch",branch:"new-branch",startFromOrigin:false} for a new worktree based on local commits, or {type:"existing_worktree",worktreePath:"/absolute/path",branch:"existing-branch"} to use an existing checkout. For upstream commits, set startFromOrigin:true. Omitted workspaceStrategy means the project root, NOT the caller's worktree. Omit projectId/modelSelection/modes to inherit those settings from the calling thread; a caller outside a T3 thread must pass projectId and gets the project's default model. Set scratch:true instead of projectId for a thread without a project: it runs in a fresh folder of its own, outside any repository. Put the task in message. Do not ask the agent to create its own worktree via shell: that does not update the thread binding. Each call creates a new launch with no retry key; retain threadId and use t3_thread_read/t3_thread_wait to follow preparation. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title. After errors or lost responses, inspect t3_thread_list before retrying. Attachments must be pending uploads. The new thread may not run with broader runtime or interaction modes than the caller: the calling T3 thread's own modes, or the permission mode an outside agent was approved with.

T3 Code checks it every two minutes and wakes you with a message when a check fails, the required checks pass, someone else comments or reviews, or the branch starts to conflict with its base. Use this to monitor or babysit a pull request instead of polling, sleeping, or running a watcher. Only comments posted after this call wake you, so handle the existing ones first, then end your turn. A wake is news, not a merge decision: check readiness yourself before merging. While T3 Code watches, the thread stays in the user's Working list, not their inbox. When you hand the work back to the user, call unwatch_pull_request first so the thread returns to their inbox. Watching ends when the pull request merges or closes, when its thread settles or is archived, when T3 Code fails to read it 8 times in a row (a host rate limit only delays it), when the user stops this thread, or when you call unwatch_pull_request. Unsettle the thread before starting a new watch. A subagent cannot watch: its parent thread owns the pull request.

Work on a whole sentence

Morgan's opening line has been rewritten nine times. Sentence bench keeps the working wording at the top with Use this wording beside it. Rewrite lists complete earlier wordings, rule-based changes and model alternatives, each with its word-count change. Choose one to make it the working wording, or Compare to keep the original alongside. Hover or keyboard-focus a candidate to preview it in place on the page. How these were checked shows the grammar status and any meaning the check could not verify. Undo restores the edit.

Words offers bundled thesaurus choices shown inside the full sentence, and underlines words you have already used in the paragraph. A synonym can change the meaning, so read the sentence again. With the Words in context pack installed, On-device alternatives adds local word predictions. Likely is not the same as right.

Place shows where else the sentence could sit, with the sentences on either side. Read each arrangement before choosing Move here; the reasons come from local rules and no model has judged them. Hear reads the sentence before, the working wording and the sentence after through your narration player, using a downloaded local voice or your voice service.

Follow a thread

Threads pairs exact sentences from the manuscript that may be talking to each other. Hover or keyboard-focus a pair to mark both passages; choose a sentence to go to it. Local checks find repeated wording, shared vocabulary and possible references. A relation stays unverified until the judgement service has read it; a model reading names its source and shows how sure it is.

For an exact repeat, you can remove either occurrence as one undoable edit. Repetition is sometimes the point, so leaving both is always an option. If the passage changes, reopen the instrument before trusting its earlier reading.

Follow an entity through the piece

In the instrument desk, choose Entities. Select a name candidate to see every mention across the sections and read the source passages. The index is local and literal: it can include places or ordinary capitalised words, and a candidate is not a confirmed character. Spelling variants are grouped by a local rule.

Choose a reading, then Read with judgement model to inspect relationships by section, compare a named attribute such as the colour of a coat, or try blind dialogue attribution. The blind reading hides speaker tags and is allowed to answer Unknown. Every result keeps its exact evidence and full distribution. A possible contradiction is a lead to chase, and a model's confidence is not a grade for your characterisation.

Read paragraphs; keep your choices

Open Paragraph readings in The piece to see each paragraph's scores and narrating tense. Local English cues and Jev readings are labelled separately so you know which is which. Inspect distributions and context shows the exact paragraph behind a reading, including a split or uncertain result. These readings stand apart from the whole-piece grade and its estimate.

Keeping a deliberate style or name exception saves the existing uses in the folio's Charter. New drift can still be flagged. Check these again removes the exception. A save notice tells you if the choice could only be kept on this device.

Invite an editor into the work

Sentence bench, each Threads pair and Scene bench offer Ask the room. Your judgement model, Jev when selected, reads the passage, your working proposal and the tool's question, then chooses the editor most likely to help. It may choose no one. You can also pick an editor yourself.

Read the implementation map above for present behavior. ## The problem in one paragraph Twyne's help is shaped like notifications. Local rules decide that something might be worth saying, Jev decides whether to say it, and a card describes it in the margin. Most cards _describe_ ("You wrote", "Possible repetition", "Say it plainly first") instead of _doing_ something to the text. Without a prose model the tools have almost nothing to offer: they show the writer's own fragments back to them and suggest connecting a model. Jev, the cheapest and fastest model available, is used mostly as a yes/no gate in front of cards. Splitting, joining, or moving a sentence erases its history. With sentence IDs as the options, Jev can point to _where_: which sentence this depends on, where this sentence fits, and which earlier line it repeats. None of the proposals use this. - **They ignore other modalities.** Listening to prose read aloud is the oldest revision technique there is, and Twyne already includes a local TTS model. - **They don't fix the foundation.** Positional identity, polluted attempts, fragile 14-word regex anchors, and the Convex-client gate in front of the writer's own judgement endpoint (`struggle-tracker.ts` `ask`: `if (!client) throw new Error("offline")`) would also undermine every new card. Examples: grammar (Harper, already shipped), word alternatives, words a model finds unlikely in context, repetition. All of these run locally. 2. **Between lines (threads).** Typed links between spans: _repeats, sets up, pays off, supports, contradicts, answers, refers back to_. content.content:
The critique and capability ladder below describe the starting point and intended direction. Read the implementation map above for present behavior.

## The problem in one paragraph

Twyne's help is shaped like notifications. Local rules decide that something might be worth saying, Jev decides whether to say it, and a card describes it in the margin. Most cards _describe_ ("You wrote", "Possible repetition", "Say it plainly first") instead of _doing_ something to the text. Without a prose model the tools have almost nothing to offer: they show the writer's own fragments back to them and suggest connecting a model. Jev, the cheapest and fastest model available, is used mostly as a yes/no gate in front of cards. It is rarely used to point at spans, choose a position, or rank candidates, which is what it does best.

## Why Sentence Lab feels broken (verified in code)

1. **The "earlier tries" are mid-edit snapshots, not attempts.** `struggle-tracker.ts:85` commits a version after every 1.2 s pause, and `commitVersion` (`struggle-signals.ts`) stores the previous wording whenever exactly one sentence changed. A pause in the middle of a word records something like `The river carr the town's memory.` as an attempt.
2. **Sentence identity depends on position.** When the paragraph's sentence count changes, `commitVersion` clears `rewrites` and `attempts`. Splitting, joining, or moving a sentence erases its history. Activity is keyed by block position, so moving a sentence elsewhere is not visible at all.
3. **Without a prose provider there is nothing to show.** `fillSpec` (`in-flow-tools.ts`) returns the seed and the notice "Your own attempts only — connect a model in Settings for fresh variants." The tool's main content then comes from item 1.
4. **The variants carry no reasons.** The prompt asks for three different approaches (reorder, cut, make concrete), but the UI labels them all "Other ways". Nothing checks whether a variant keeps the meaning.
5. **The tool covers only wording.** It has no word-level alternatives, no placement, no read-aloud, and no comparison in context.

## Critique of the proposed cards in `audit.md`

| Proposal                   | Keep                                                                                 | Problem                                                                                       | Change                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Three ways forward         | The core idea: complete alternatives you can choose, edit, compare, or keep original | The generator labels its own variants ("Shorter"); it needs a prose model; it is still a card | Code computes facts like word count and voice; Jev or embeddings check meaning; rule-based rewrites and on-device models fill it offline |
| Find the exact word        | Yes                                                                                  | Assumes an LLM                                                                                | Works offline: thesaurus candidates ranked by a small masked language model in context; Jev adds nuance tags                             |
| Evidence with limits       | Yes, later                                                                           | Large dependency on fetching sources                                                          | Leave in research; reuse the claim span from the Threads index                                                                           |
| Show the shape             | Yes                                                                                  | "Constrained schema" still lets a model invent nodes                                          | Every node must be a span of the writer's text. Jev picks spans and edge types; code draws                                               |
| One concrete example       | Partly                                                                               | Invented examples are a hallucination risk in nonfiction                                      | Offer only sourced examples, the writer's own notebook scraps, or examples clearly labelled hypothetical                                 |
| Bridge these two thoughts  | Yes                                                                                  | No trigger defined                                                                            | A drop in embedding similarity between neighbours is the trigger; Jev names the relation; the LLM drafts a transition                    |
| Recover the useful attempt | Yes                                                                                  | Depends on attempt history, which is currently corrupted (see above)                          | Fix capture first                                                                                                                        |
| A next step you choose     | No                                                                                   | Still general coaching                                                                        | Replace with **Say it**: the writer speaks what they mean and the transcript becomes a candidate sentence                                |

Gaps shared by every proposal:

- **They remain cards.** None of them changes where help appears. Everything still lives in a margin column, away from the words it concerns.
- **They don't cover the offline case.** Every useful proposal assumes a prose LLM, and that is the main complaint.
- **They use Jev only as a gate.** Jev can choose among up to 255 IDs in one question (the TypeSafe "line-by-line search" cookbook pattern). With sentence IDs as the options, Jev can point to _where_: which sentence this depends on, where this sentence fits, and which earlier line it repeats. None of the proposals use this.
- **They ignore other modalities.** Listening to prose read aloud is the oldest revision technique there is, and Twyne already includes a local TTS model.
- **They don't fix the foundation.** Positional identity, polluted attempts, fragile 14-word regex anchors, and the Convex-client gate in front of the writer's own judgement endpoint (`struggle-tracker.ts` `ask`: `if (!client) throw new Error("offline")`) would also undermine every new card.

What the audit gets right and should be kept: label each suggestion's provenance (rule, judgement model, text model, external lookup), give the writer control over when things appear, and measure applied edits instead of card opens.

## The reframe: three places help can live

Replace "cards" with **instruments**: tools that point at a span and change it, always with a preview and undo.

1. **In the line.** Underlines, ghost text, and small glyphs placed directly in the manuscript, like Grammarly but for a literary writer. Examples: grammar (Harper, already shipped), word alternatives, words a model finds unlikely in context, repetition. All of these run locally.
2. **Between lines (threads).** Typed links between spans: _repeats, sets up, pays off, supports, contradicts, answers, refers back to_. They appear when the writer selects or hovers with a modifier key, or when a "Threads" lens is turned on. The critique and capability ladder below describe the starting point and intended direction. Read the implementation map above for present behavior.

## The problem in one paragraph

Twyne's help is shaped like notifications. Local rules decide that something might be worth saying, Jev decides whether to say it, and a card describes it in the margin. Most cards _describe_ ("You wrote", "Possible repetition", "Say it plainly first") instead of _doing_ something to the text. Without a prose model the tools have almost nothing to offer: they show the writer's own fragments back to them and suggest connecting a model. Jev, the cheapest and fastest model available, is used mostly as a yes/no gate in front of cards. It is rarely used to point at spans, choose a position, or rank candidates, which is what it does best.

## Why Sentence Lab feels broken (verified in code)

1. **The "earlier tries" are mid-edit snapshots, not attempts.** `struggle-tracker.ts:85` commits a version after every 1.2 s pause, and `commitVersion` (`struggle-signals.ts`) stores the previous wording whenever exactly one sentence changed. A pause in the middle of a word records something like `The river carr the town's memory.` as an attempt.
2. **Sentence identity depends on position.** When the paragraph's sentence count changes, `commitVersion` clears `rewrites` and `attempts`. Splitting, joining, or moving a sentence erases its history. Activity is keyed by block position, so moving a sentence elsewhere is not visible at all.
3. **Without a prose provider there is nothing to show.** `fillSpec` (`in-flow-tools.ts`) returns the seed and the notice "Your own attempts only — connect a model in Settings for fresh variants." The tool's main content then comes from item 1.
4. **The variants carry no reasons.** The prompt asks for three different approaches (reorder, cut, make concrete), but the UI labels them all "Other ways". Nothing checks whether a variant keeps the meaning.
5. **The tool covers only wording.** It has no word-level alternatives, no placement, no read-aloud, and no comparison in context.

## Critique of the proposed cards in `audit.md`

| Proposal                   | Keep                                                                                 | Problem                                                                                       | Change                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Three ways forward         | The core idea: complete alternatives you can choose, edit, compare, or keep original | The generator labels its own variants ("Shorter"); it needs a prose model; it is still a card | Code computes facts like word count and voice; Jev or embeddings check meaning; rule-based rewrites and on-device models fill it offline |
| Find the exact word        | Yes                                                                                  | Assumes an LLM                                                                                | Works offline: thesaurus candidates ranked by a small masked language model in context; Jev adds nuance tags                             |
| Evidence with limits       | Yes, later                                                                           | Large dependency on fetching sources                                                          | Leave in research; reuse the claim span from the Threads index                                                                           |
| Show the shape             | Yes                                                                                  | "Constrained schema" still lets a model invent nodes                                          | Every node must be a span of the writer's text. Jev picks spans and edge types; code draws                                               |
| One concrete example       | Partly                                                                               | Invented examples are a hallucination risk in nonfiction                                      | Offer only sourced examples, the writer's own notebook scraps, or examples clearly labelled hypothetical                                 |
| Bridge these two thoughts  | Yes                                                                                  | No trigger defined                                                                            | A drop in embedding similarity between neighbours is the trigger; Jev names the relation; the LLM drafts a transition                    |
| Recover the useful attempt | Yes                                                                                  | Depends on attempt history, which is currently corrupted (see above)                          | Fix capture first                                                                                                                        |
| A next step you choose     | No                                                                                   | Still general coaching                                                                        | Replace with **Say it**: the writer speaks what they mean and the transcript becomes a candidate sentence                                |

Gaps shared by every proposal:

- **They remain cards.** None of them changes where help appears. Everything still lives in a margin column, away from the words it concerns.
- **They don't cover the offline case.** Every useful proposal assumes a prose LLM, and that is the main complaint.
- **They use Jev only as a gate.** Jev can choose among up to 255 IDs in one question (the TypeSafe "line-by-line search" cookbook pattern). With sentence IDs as the options, Jev can point to _where_: which sentence this depends on, where this sentence fits, and which earlier line it repeats. None of the proposals use this.
- **They ignore other modalities.** Listening to prose read aloud is the oldest revision technique there is, and Twyne already includes a local TTS model.
- **They don't fix the foundation.** Positional identity, polluted attempts, fragile 14-word regex anchors, and the Convex-client gate in front of the writer's own judgement endpoint (`struggle-tracker.ts` `ask`: `if (!client) throw new Error("offline")`) would also undermine every new card.

What the audit gets right and should be kept: label each suggestion's provenance (rule, judgement model, text model, external lookup), give the writer control over when things appear, and measure applied edits instead of card opens.

## The reframe: three places help can live

Replace "cards" with **instruments**: tools that point at a span and change it, always with a preview and undo.

1. **In the line.** Underlines, ghost text, and small glyphs placed directly in the manuscript, like Grammarly but for a literary writer. Examples: grammar (Harper, already shipped), word alternatives, words a model finds unlikely in context, repetition. All of these run locally.
2. **Between lines (threads).** Typed links between spans: _repeats, sets up, pays off, supports, contradicts, answers, refers back to_. They appear when the writer selects or hovers with a modifier key, or when a "Threads" lens is turned on. The curve-drawing code in `flow-surface.tsx` already draws card-to-passage links; extend it to draw sentence-to-sentence links with labels.
3. **On the bench.** A focused workbench opened on one span: the Sentence bench, the Paragraph bench, and the Scene bench (described below).

**Surfacing rule.** Nothing appears automatically unless it carries a change ready to apply or opens a working instrument with one click. Pure information ("You wrote this earlier") is not allowed. The current echo card either becomes **Recover**, which offers a concrete merge, or a **thread**, which names the relationship.

content.content:
**ABScribe: Summary**

**What it does:** ABScribe is an interface for human-AI co-writing. It helps writers generate and manage several alternative versions of text with large language models. It addresses a problem with current tools: making new versions tends to either overwrite the original or clutter the document with pasted alternatives. ABScribe supports exploration that is "rapid, yet visually structured." Users revise variations through LLM prompts, which the system automatically turns into reusable buttons.

**Key interaction:** "Variations are stored adjacently within text fields," so alternatives stay in place instead of piling up in the document. Writers compare them directly in context through "mouse-over interactions on a popup toolbar."

**Study size:** 12 writers, compared against a popular baseline workflow.

**Main findings:**
- ABScribe "significantly reduces task workload (d = 1.20, p < 0.001)"
- It "enhances user perceptions of the revision process (d = 2.41, p < 0.001)"
- The study also "provides insights into how writers explore variations using LLMs"

The paper appeared at CHI 2024.

Because it isn't the creative-writing paper, I can't summarize what kinds of help writers want or reject, including findings on ownership or word-level help. Nothing on this page covers those topics.

**What this paper does cover, according to its abstract:**

- **Focus:** It looks at the case where a "scientific AI writing assistant is deeply involved."
- **Method:** The authors build a framework for telling machine text from human text "from syntax, semantics, and pragmatics." They then examine writing style, coherence, consistency, and "argument logistics." They also test existing detection models.
- **Findings:**
  - AI can produce scientific content as accurate as human writing, but "there is still a gap in terms of depth and overall quality."
  - Machine-written scientific text "is more likely to contain errors in factual issues."
  - The two kinds of text differ in a "writing style" gap.
- **Contribution:** The authors propose detection features that are "model-agnostic and distribution-agnostic" and could apply to other domains.

The extra context appended to your message is documentation for a writing app (e.g., the Sentence bench and Threads features). It is not from either paper, so I didn't use it.

The search turned up the citation details and secondary summaries of the study. None of the results gave the article's numbers on how often each level of change was used.

**Citation and design:**
- Nancy Sommers, *College Composition and Communication*, v31 n4 p378-88 Dec 1980. DOI: 10.2307/356588. A PDF is posted at spalding.pbworks.com, and the stable JSTOR link is jstor.org/stable/356588.
- She used a case study approach. The participants were twenty freshmen from Boston University and the University of Oklahoma with SAT verbal scores from 450-600. Also included twenty experienced writers, including editors and journalists.
- Each writer wrote three essays, expressive, explanatory, and persuasive.
- The revisions were sorted into four revision operations: deletion, substitution, addition, and reordering. Also four levels of changes were identified: word, phrase, sentence, and theme.

**Word-level vs. sentence-level findings:**
- Students treated revision as merely a "rewording activity." "They did so," writes Sommers, "because they perceive words as the unit of discourse.
- One summary says students' main problem is that they focus on particular words, apart from their role in the text.
- Experienced writers described their revising as a cycle. Their drafts went through a series of addition and deletion of ideas, whether it might be a sentence or a whole paragraph.
- Overall, the study shows that experienced writers revise throughout the writing process, making deep and meaningful changes to strengthen their ideas and their overall execution, not just as a final step. The ERIC abstract concludes that the writing process is recursive rather than linear.

**From memory, not checked against these results:** I recall that students mostly made word-level changes, deletions and substitutions, which Sommers called a "thesaurus philosophy." I also recall that experienced writers most often changed things at the sentence level, mainly by adding and deleting, and paid attention to audience and the overall shape of the piece. To confirm the exact frequencies or the "thesaurus" wording, check the full text through JSTOR or the PDF.

**Title:** "Shaping Human-AI Collaboration: Varied Scaffolding Levels in Co-writing with Language Models" (arXiv:2402.11723)

**Authors:** Paramveer S. Dhillon, Somayeh Molaei, Jiaqi Li, Maximilian Golub, Shaochun Zheng, Lionel P. Robert

**Venue:** "Appearing at CHI 2024 (Honolulu, HI)"

**Study design:** The authors ran "a within-subjects field experiment with a Latin square design" with "(N=131)" participants. Each person answered argumentative writing prompts under three conditions in random order:
- "no AI assistance (control)"
- "next-sentence suggestions (low scaffolding)"
- "next-paragraph suggestions (high scaffolding)"

**Main findings:**
- **Overall pattern:** The paper reports "a U-shaped impact of scaffolding on writing quality and productivity (words/time)."
- **Sentence-level suggestions:** "low scaffolding did not significantly improve writing quality or productivity"
- **Paragraph-level suggestions:** "high scaffolding led to significant improvements, especially benefiting non-regular writers and less tech-savvy users"
- **Cognitive load:** "No significant cognitive burden was observed" with the scaffolded tools.
- **Ownership and satisfaction:** The authors found "a moderate decrease in text ownership and satisfaction." The abstract links this to the scaffolded tools in general and does not split it by sentence versus paragraph.
- **Design implication:** The authors argue for "the need for personalized scaffolding mechanisms."

The extra context about ABScribe and the editor documentation does not concern this paper, so I left it out.

**Abstract (excerpts and paraphrase)**
- **Background:** LLMs that can follow instructions and hold conversations have sparked interest in using them in support tools.
- **Study:** The authors ran a user study of 30 professional writers to test how useful modern LLMs are as writing aids.
- **Interface design:** It is based on the cognitive process model, which treats writing as goal-oriented thinking with "non-linear cognitive activities: planning, translating, and reviewing."
- **Survey:** Participants gave post-task feedback on the promise and drawbacks of LLMs as collaborators.

**Key finding on writing stages** (one sentence, split into two quotes to stay under the limit):

# Co-Writing with AI, on Human Terms (arXiv:2504.12488)

**Authors:** Mohi Reza, Jeb Thomas-Mitchell, Peter Dushniku, Nathan Laundry, Joseph Jay Williams, Anastasia Kuzminykh

**Venue:** PACMHCI (CSCW 2025), DOI 10.1145/3757566. The arXiv version is v2, revised 18 Aug 2025.

**Research question:** The paper asks "how to preserve writers' sense of agency and ownership when using these tools."

**Method:** The authors did a PRISMA systematic review of 109 HCI papers and interviewed 15 writers from different fields.

**Design strategies identified:** "structured guidance, guided exploration, active co-writing, and critical feedback." These are mapped onto "planning, translating, reviewing, and monitoring."

**Key findings on what writers want:**
- **Control depends on the stage of writing.** "Our findings reveal that writers' desired levels of AI intervention vary across the writing process."
- **Content-focused writers** "(e.g., academics) prioritize ownership during planning." They want to keep the ideas their own.
- **Form-focused writers** "(e.g., creatives) value control over translating and reviewing." They want authority over the actual prose and its revision.
- **Context matters.** Preferences also depend on "contextual goals, values, and notions of originality and authorship."
- **Research vs. user needs.** The study finds both alignment and gaps between existing research and what writers need.

**Caveat:** The abstract never uses the word "voice" and doesn't directly contrast feedback with generation. Those ideas only come through indirectly, in the form-focused writers' wish to control translating and reviewing and in the "critical feedback" strategy.

**Related context from earlier:**
- **ABScribe (CHI 2024, also involving Reza):** It supports revising text with AI-generated variations and "significantly reduces task workload (d = 1.20, p < 0.001)."
- **Chakrabarty et al.:** Professional writers find LLMs "more helpful in translation and reviewing."

I'm figuring out what this feature actually does: it triggers either through a selection toolbar with "Rework" for multiword selections or "Alternatives" for single words, opening a bench that operates on a single sentence even when a whole passage was selected—revealing a mismatch. It also triggers automatically when the struggle tracker detects the same sentence being reworded three or more times.

The deeper issue is that this tool answers a different problem than the one writers actually have—when someone rewrites a sentence nine times, the sentence usually isn't wrong at the word level, it's that the writer hasn't figured out what job the sentence needs to do.

Drawing on Sommers' research, novice revision is reword-driven while experienced revision is recursive and idea/reader-driven, and this bench is really just building the novice's tool: a thesaurus plus wordiness rules. The local regex rules also rarely fire on real literary prose since phrases like "in order to" aren't what people agonize over—the fixture sentence used to demonstrate the tool is a strawman, and the bundled 45-word thesaurus offers insult-level suggestions (like "walked→strolled") for serious writers. Worse, the candidates ignore the writer's own reasoning for rewording in the first place—the attempt history is the only writer-specific signal available, yet it's displayed as just another option rather than as evidence of intent.

Then there's the interface itself: four tabs plus compare, context, whole paragraph, ask editor, and disclosures amount to an instrument panel where the writer has to diagnose their own problem before even getting help—that's the hardest part, and it's punted onto the user. The caveat culture bothers me too, with "meaning has not been checked" stamped on every candidate reflexively. When a model is involved, the prompt is a generic "give 3 alternatives, keep meaning and register," which is the classic AI rewrite-picker pattern that research (Dhillon et al.) found doesn't actually improve quality for this kind of task, and it undermines writer ownership since form-focused writers want control, not translation (per Reza et al.). The "Place" tab just enumerates slots without judgment when the writer could simply cut and paste, "Hear" duplicates existing "Hear it read" functionality, and selecting "Rework" on a passage silently narrows scope to a single sentence without telling the writer. What's actually worth keeping is the ledger of the writer's own past wordings.

Now I'm thinking through what's genuinely valuable: the sentence-history ledger is a unique asset no other tool has, tracking that you've written a given sentence nine different ways. The in-place ghost preview with neighboring context, diffing, single-undo apply, and staleness checks all seem solid, as does hearing a sentence read in context with its neighbors—reading aloud is a legitimate revision technique—plus the persona room.

I want to reframe the whole feature from "generate alternatives" to "settle the sentence"—the bench should help the writer decide what the sentence needs to do, using their own past attempts as raw material, then let them commit and move on. Thinking about naming it something like "Settle this sentence" or "Line under pressure." For the trigger mechanic, I'm weighing whether this should surface automatically once the ledger shows three or more settled wordings of the same sentence, maybe as a small margin glyph rather than a full four-tab panel, while reconciling that against the autonomy-by-default principle that features should run without clicks and buttons should be optional overrides.

I'm also reconciling this against the surfacing rule that nothing should appear automatically unless it carries a ready-to-apply change or opens a working instrument in one click—so the glyph itself satisfies that by opening the instrument instantly, even though the analysis behind it runs invisibly in the background. For manual triggering, selecting a sentence could offer a "Rework" or renamed "Settle" action, while single-word selections keep a lighter inline popover rather than the full bench. The bench's inputs would be the sentence's full wording ledger with timestamps, its neighboring sentences for handoff context, the paragraph, the project's goal/audience, and optionally a persona—feeding into a "Versions" view that stacks the writer's own past wordings oldest to newest, each diffed against the current version, emphasizing that these are the writer's own attempts, not AI-generated alternatives.

Above that list, I want one line that names what's constant versus what keeps shifting across versions—computed purely through token alignment (like an LCS comparison) rather than a model call, surfacing exactly what the writer is actually deciding between. Optionally, a model could add a single framing sentence naming the underlying choice (e.g., agent vs. container verb framing) without slipping into full AI rewriting, and the writer could then splice elements from their own versions together, like taking a verb from one draft and a sentence order from another.

For the decision step itself: the writer can settle on a version (archiving the rest), splice fragments, or park the sentence — committing current wording while flagging it as unsettled with alternates attached for a later pass, so no single sentence blocks the draft. This mirrors the common "TK" or bracketed-alternates practice writers already use, though I should flag that as inferred practice rather than a sourced claim.

For scope, I want to trim the regex-based rewrite rules from the bench (letting a Harper-style linter handle those) and separate out the bundled thesaurus from the main review flow, keeping a single-word alternatives popover as its own lightweight feature rather than a full thesaurus panel.

Beyond that, I'm cutting the Words tab, the unjudged-slot auto-open behavior, the generic "3 alternatives" framing, the disclosure/likelihood caveats, and the compare side panel in favor of a stacked version diff — essentially stripping tabs entirely. What survives is the core: the working textarea, a hover ghost preview, an A/B hear comparison, and a single-question "ask an editor" feature.

For a small implementable v1: build a version stack from the ledger's existing wordings plus the current text, computing contested vs. constant tokens via a multi-diff against current (reusing the sentence word-diff logic) and highlighting contested spans. Each version gets Use and Hear-vs-current actions using existing applyVariant/hearVariant functions, though Hear needs sequential A/B playback. Parking a version means applying current while flagging alternates on the ledger entry with a margin glyph — but since the ledger is session-local, persistence of parked versions becomes its own scope question.

I'm also noting that persisting parked alternates via a comment-mark extension could work (inserting a user comment listing alternates, which survives reload and shows in the margin), though since another agent may currently be editing comment-mark files, I should just propose this rather than touch it myself. I also want to simplify the bench UI by removing tabs/rules/thesaurus/place, keeping single-word alternatives as a separate popover or dropping them, and rethinking the auto-trigger behavior — instead of auto-opening the panel at three or more wordings, show a margin glyph like "9 versions" instead, which means checking whether the tracker's auto-open currently sets an active state directly.

I'm also considering the edge case where a writer reworks a fresh sentence with no history: the bench could let them type their own alternate versions into a stack, or have the model state the sentence's required job in one line without rewriting it, with model-generated variants as a last resort.

For v1, I'd lean toward skipping model rewrites entirely and having the model's main job be naming the decision — though that tradeoff means less-experienced writers lose a quick-fix option that scaffolding research (Dhillon) suggests helps them most. I want to name that tradeoff explicitly and sketch a realistic before/after journey, maybe an essay writer using something like Twyne.

Imagining the concrete scenario: a writer rewrites a sentence about a river six times, and the tool's bench shows candidates from their own past versions as diffs, flags an unused word, and offers no model suggestion — just a note that meaning hasn't been checked. They close it and rewrite a seventh time anyway. In an alternate version with model suggestions, three AI rewrites appear in a voice that isn't theirs, and the writer picks none of them — which tells me the after-state should surface something like a margin marker showing "6 versions" to make the revision history visible without replacing the writer's own judgment.

Or the glyph just becomes a quiet marker and drafting resumes. For evaluation, I want behavioral instrumentation tracking how often the bench leads to settle/use/park within session versus simply closing without resolution.

Also worth checking whether a sentence gets re-edited soon after being settled, how fast the writer returns to drafting elsewhere, and whether they end up choosing their own version over model text — this last one being a proxy for ownership. For the qualitative side, dogfooding on the user's own manuscripts is key since they've said they can't picture using this; the real test is whether they reach for it unprompted within a week.

I'm also flagging a risk: ledger histories might be too thin or noisy since they're session-local with a 5-second settle window, and sentence identity can break across edits/splits — if most struggling sentences don't have at least a few clean versions, there's nothing for the feature to work with, so this needs validating against real sessions before building anything. There's also the problem that session-local history disappears on reload, which conflicts with the fact that revision often happens the next day — persisting it would expand scope and raise privacy considerations around data movement.

Beyond that, I'm weighing whether contested-span summaries hold up when versions are restructured wholesale (LCS alignment could fail, so falling back to a simple stack makes sense), whether removing Words/Place strips away functionality people rely on, and whether "decision naming" is still too close to model judgment and risks confident misreading, even if it's less invasive than full prose. I'm also considering autonomy tensions like auto-opening during flow state, and interference cases like another agent editing comment-mark files or persona cards changing underneath an "Ask an editor" feature. Pushing back on my own recommendation, I wonder if the better move is scrapping the Sentence Bench altogether and folding "Hear in context" plus version history directly into the ledger's inline UI.

Challenging whether a bench is even needed: the strongest counter is that users won't gravitate to sentence-level tools since their real need sits at the paragraph/argument level — Claim Check, Reader Questions, Threads — and Sommers' research suggests experienced writers revise at higher levels anyway, so my workflow might only serve a narrow moment. A writer stuck rewriting one sentence nine times may need to be nudged to move on (Park) more than handed a better tool, which makes me think "Park" deserves to be the central action, and the minimal design might just be an inline "keep both and move on" affordance with no bench at all. I'm also questioning whether the "constant vs contested" framing is genuinely useful or just a clever-looking visualization built on inference, since the only real evidence I have is for diff stacks reducing workload in a different context (LLM-generated variations, not a writer's own versions).

There are still several unresolved tradeoffs I need to work through: auto-open versus a glyph trigger, whether to drop model rewrites entirely or keep them as a gated option, how ledger versions should persist (local IndexedDB, synced, or neither) given privacy concerns, where single-word alternatives should live in the UI, and whether Park should use comment marks or a new annotation type. I also caught a bug — selecting "Rework" across a multi-sentence passage silently narrows to just one sentence, so I need to route multi-sentence selections to passage-level tools instead or clearly indicate which sentence was chosen. Before moving on I want to verify a couple of implementation facts: whether ledger entries are recorded only after the five-second settle delay, and whether the ledger persists beyond a session or is scoped per comment.

# Sentence Bench: research and recommendation (Opus, round 1)

I didn't edit any files. Everything below comes from reading the code at `/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne` plus the external papers cited at the end. I didn't find an Impeccable skill in the repo. This is workflow research rather than visual design, so I went ahead without it.

## 1. What the feature actually does

**How it opens**
- **From a selection.** Selecting text shows **Rework** (several words) or **Alternatives** (one word) in the selection toolbar (`selection-actions.tsx:210-217`). This calls `openKind("sentence-lab", text)`, which narrows to a single sentence: the one at the cursor, a text match, or the paragraph's longest (`struggle-tracker.ts:1412+`, `in-flow-tools.ts:203`). If you select a whole passage and click Rework, you quietly get a bench for one sentence of it.
- **Automatically, after rewording.** It opens when the struggle tracker sees the same sentence reworded 3 or more times. Jev decides whether to show it, and if Jev is unavailable the tracker shows it anyway because the local signal is strong enough (`struggle-signals.ts`, `audit.md:239`).
- **Automatically, after moving.** It opens on the Place tab when a sentence has been moved to 3 or more positions (`struggle-tracker.ts:318-336`).

**What's on the bench** (`sentence-bench.tsx`, `utils/sentence-bench.ts`)
- **Rewrite tab.** Up to 8 local candidates:
  - the writer's earlier "settled" wordings, taken from the sentence ledger;
  - 11 regex wordiness rules ("in order to" → "to", "made a decision to" → "decided to");
  - removing "really/very";
  - splitting at a semicolon;
  - moving a trailing "before/after/when" clause to the front.

  If a prose model is connected, it adds up to 3 alternatives from a generic prompt ("keep its meaning and register… reorder, cut, make concrete"). Every candidate is grammar-checked with Harper, shown as a diff with a word-count change, previewed as ghost text on hover, and carries an "About" disclosure full of caveats.
- **Words tab.** A hand-written thesaurus of roughly 45 headwords (walked → strolled/strode/wandered, good → sound/effective/valuable). There's also an optional on-device word-prediction model that shows a likelihood score.
- **Place tab.** Every neighbouring position in the same paragraph, generated by rule. The panel itself says "Their fit has not been judged."
- **Hear tab.** Text-to-speech of the sentence before, the working wording, and the sentence after.
- **Around the tabs.** Compare, Context, Whole paragraph, and Ask an editor (one persona comment).
- **Applying.** "Use this wording" applies the change with one undo and a stale-text check.

**Facts that limit it**
- The sentence ledger lives only in memory inside the struggle tracker; no other source file uses it. Version history is gone after a reload, which is usually when revision happens.
- The fixture sentence ("We made a decision to leave in order to find a very quiet room.") is written to trigger the rules. Sentences people actually agonise over almost never contain "in order to".

## 2. Why a writer would or wouldn't use it

**Why not (my inference from the code, not user research):**
1. **It answers the wrong question.** Rewording a sentence nine times rarely means the wording has a mechanical fault. Usually the writer hasn't decided what the sentence has to do: what it takes over from the sentence before and what it sets up for the one after. Wordiness rules and a thesaurus fix clutter, which the writer could fix alone.
2. **The writer has to diagnose the problem first.** Four tabs plus Compare, Context, Whole paragraph, Ask an editor and the About disclosures mean choosing between Rewrite, Words, Place and Hear before getting any help. That diagnosis is the hard part.
3. **Its most valuable data is just another list item.** No other tool knows "you've written this sentence six ways," yet the bench shows those versions as candidates beside regex output. It doesn't use them as evidence of what the writer is deciding between.
4. **With a model, it becomes the generic rewrite picker.** Three wordings in someone else's voice. Reza et al. find that form-focused writers, such as creative writers, want control over drafting and revision. Dhillon et al. found next-sentence suggestions didn't improve quality or productivity. That finding is adjacent rather than direct, because they tested continuation, not rewording.
5. **Caveats on every row.** "Meaning has not been checked" is repeated throughout. This is the reflexive hedging the project already wants to avoid.
6. **Place and Hear add little.** Place lists positions without judging them, which isn't much better than cut and paste. Hear duplicates "Hear it read".

**Why a writer would use it:** in-place ghost preview between the real neighbouring sentences, a one-undo apply, hearing the sentence in context, and the ledger of the writer's own versions. Those are worth keeping.

## 3. Recommendation: from "suggest alternatives" to "settle this sentence"

The job is to help the writer **decide between versions they've already written, or park the decision and keep drafting**. It isn't to generate more versions.

**Trigger**
- Same signal as today: a sentence with 3 or more settled wordings in the ledger.
- Change what appears: a quiet margin mark ("6 versions") instead of a four-tab panel opening mid-flow. The analysis runs on its own, which matches the autonomy-by-default memory. Opening it takes one click or one keystroke.
- Manually: Rework on a selection of **one** sentence. If the selection spans several sentences, offer the passage tools instead of quietly narrowing to one.

**Input and context**
- The ledger's wordings for the sentence, plus the current one.
- The sentence before and the sentence after.
- The brief's goal and audience. These are already passed to `classify` and `fillSpec`.

**What the writer sees**
1. The current sentence in place, with its neighbours shown faintly above and below.
2. One computed line (local, no model), built by aligning every version against the current one with the existing `sentenceWordDiff`. For example: *"Same in all 6: river · town · memory. Still changing: the verb (carries / holds / keeps) and the ending."* This names the decision the writer is circling.
3. The versions stacked oldest to newest, with the changing parts highlighted. Hovering shows the ghost preview in the page, which already exists.
4. If a model is connected, one sentence that frames the choice instead of a rewrite. For example: *"These differ on whether the river acts on the town or stores it; your next sentence ('Every spring it gives something back') assumes it acts."* No new prose is generated.

**What the writer decides**
- **Use** a version. This calls the existing `applyVariant`.
- **Hear A/B.** The current version, then the chosen one, each between the same neighbours. This extends `hearVariant` to play two in sequence.
- **Edit** in the working field. Each edit adds to the stack.
- **Park.** Keep the current wording and attach the runner-up versions to the sentence as a note. The margin mark changes from "versions" to "parked". This is the action I'd treat as most important: it lets one sentence stop holding up the draft.

**Back to the manuscript:** Use or Park closes the bench, returns focus to the editor with the cursor at the start of the next sentence, and stops the trigger from firing again for this sentence.

## 4. Before and after: one realistic session

**Before.** Morgan is drafting an essay opening and has reworded its second sentence six times. Rewrite opens on its own. No rule applies. Five earlier versions are listed as diffs beside "Read in context; meaning has not been checked." "Carries" isn't in the Words thesaurus. Place lists three positions. Morgan closes the panel and rewrites a seventh time. With a model connected, three polished rewrites appear in a register that isn't Morgan's, and Morgan picks none of them.

**After.** A "6 versions" mark appears beside the sentence. Morgan clicks it. The bench says *the verb keeps changing (carries / holds / keeps); everything else is settled*. Morgan hovers version 3 and sees it in the page, then hears the current version and version 3 back to back between the real neighbours. Morgan picks version 3 and clicks Use. The bench closes and the cursor sits at the next sentence. On a different day Morgan can't decide, clicks Park, and keeps drafting. The alternative waits on the sentence for the revision pass.

## 5. What to remove
- The regex wordiness rules as candidates. Harper and the inline lint layer are the right home for them, if they're kept at all.
- The Words tab and its 45-word thesaurus. Single-word **Alternatives** needs its own small inline popover or should be dropped. That's an unresolved choice (see §8).
- The Place tab and the automatic opening after 3 moves. The ledger can keep tracking moves without offering them.
- The generic "3 alternative wordings" model prompt.
- The tabs, the Compare panel (the version stack replaces it), the About disclosures, the per-candidate caveats and the likelihood numbers.
- **Keep:** the working field, ghost preview, one-undo apply, stale checks, Hear (now A/B), and Ask an editor, rephrased as "Which version does this job here?"

## 6. Small scope that could ship
1. Build the version stack from `ledger.entries[].wordings` with a "same / still changing" summary using `sentenceWordDiff`. When the versions don't align (the sentence was fully restructured), show only the stack.
2. Per-version Use and Hear A/B, reusing `applyVariant`, `previewVariant` and `hearVariant`.
3. Park, implemented as an ordinary user comment on the sentence that lists the alternatives. This reuses comment infrastructure, persists across reloads and shows in the margin. **Coordination:** `comment-mark.ts` is currently modified in the working tree, so this should wait for the persona-card work to land.
4. Remove the tabs and content listed in §5.
5. Make multi-sentence Rework route to the passage tools.

The optional model "decision" line is a follow-up, not part of v1.

## 7. How to evaluate it

**Before building:** sample real ledger histories from the user's own sessions. If most struggling sentences don't have 3 or more clean versions (the ledger waits 5 s before counting a wording as settled, and history is in memory only), the feature has nothing to work with and the plan should change.

**Behaviour, measured locally:**
- After the bench opens on a struggle sentence: the share of opens that end in Use or Park versus closing without acting.
- Re-struggle rate: is the sentence reworded again within about 10 minutes of being settled? Lower is better.
- Time until the writer is typing elsewhere.
- The share of applied wordings that are the writer's own.

**The real test:** does the user reach for it on their own manuscript within a week without being prompted?

**Correctness:** fixture tests for the "same / still changing" summary using real version histories, not the rule-bait sentence.

## 8. Challenging this recommendation, and open tradeoffs
- **The bench may be the wrong layer altogether.** Experienced writers mostly revise at the level of ideas and the reader, not words (Sommers, 1980; details in Sources). The honest alternative recommendation is **no bench at all**: an inline "6 versions · hear · park" affordance on the sentence, with the effort moved to the paragraph tools (Claim Check, Reader Questions, Threads). My proposal is already half that. The cross-critique round should push on whether the panel needs to exist.
- **The "same / still changing" summary is untested.** It could be a clever display that tells the writer what they already know. The evidence for a stack of adjacent variations compared in context (ABScribe) involved LLM-generated variations, not the writer's own.
- **Removing model rewrites hurts some users.** Dhillon et al. found that higher scaffolding helped non-regular writers most. Dropping rewrites trades away a quick fix for those users in exchange for ownership.
- **Persistence.** The ledger is in memory only. Persisting versions (locally, or synced) is the bigger and more valuable change, but it raises a "where does this data go" question that PRODUCT.md says must be made explicit.
- **Auto-open versus a margin mark.** A mark is quieter, but autonomy-by-default argues for showing the analysis without a click.
- **Single-word Alternatives** needs a home or a decision to cut it.
- **Park as a comment** reuses existing infrastructure, but it mixes machine-made alternatives with human comments. A dedicated annotation type would be cleaner and larger.
- **The model's decision line is still a model judgement.** It may confidently misread the sentence. It intrudes on ownership less than generated prose does, but it isn't free.

## Sources
